newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Credit Lyonnais aid revives debate on EU control.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais aid revives debate on EU control.

text.p: The European Commission's apparent inability to stop successive, massive subsidies flowing to France's Credit Lyonnais underlines the limits the EU faces in curbing aid to ailing businesses, analysts say.
It is most clear in the banking sector where failure of a giant such as Credit Lyonnais -- once the world's largest bank outside Japan -- could have a devastating effect.

On Wednesday the Commission, the EU's competition watchdog, cleared 3.9-billion French francs ($764.5 million) in emergency aid for the state-controlled bank pending a request by French authorities for a new rescue plan. It agreed in July 1995 to a 45 billion franc bail out for the bank.
"This is a never ending story," one European competition analyst said.
Competition lawyers and EU officials said the Commission had no choice but to agree to the emergency measures and to examine a French request to change the ongoing rescue plan.

"Although this may seem outrageous, (Competition Commissioner Karel) Van Miert has no alternative but to examine the new measures and see whether they can be allowed under the rules on restructuring aid," a Brussels-based lawyer said.

Although the Commission must ensure fair competition in the 15-nation EU, it is obliged to strike a difficult balance between this objective and the desire of national governments to help large, state-controlled, companies in distress.
Under EU rules, it may allow subsidies if strictly intended to help a company get back to profitability.
It usually helps if the government concerned commits itself to privatising the company being aided, the only guarantee that the it will no longer get taxpayers money.
Van Miert made it clear on Wednesday the new plan for Lyonnnais would be subjected to a thorough examination to make sure it get things right this time.
Defending the Commission's 1995 decision, which Lyonnais' main French rivals had judged too lax, Van Miert implicitly admitted that, if anything, it had been too tough.
Only a year later the bank is again in deep trouble, due mainly to the lacklustre French financial market and the poor public image of the bank, he said.
Another French bank, Societe Generale, has challenged the Commission's 1995 decision in the European Court of Justice and Banque Nationale de Paris has also been very critical.
"(Credit Lyonnais') rivals said at the time that the Commission had not been tough enough and that it (the 1995 rescue plan) would turn the bank into a 'super champion"', Van Miert said.
"We see today that that was not the case," he added, suggesting it could be picked up for about one franc, debts and all.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said later that the bank's privatisation would happen earlier than expected, perhaps anticipating Commission conditions. The bank was originally due to be sold by 2000.

The debate over the Commission's ability to control state aid was particularly vivid in 1994 when the Commission took some spectacularly pricey decisions concerning another two French ailing companies, Air France and computer firm Bull.

In Europe, however, there appears to be few options. Competition analysts note the Commission is the institution with the power to call subsidising national governments to order. ($1=5.101 French Franc)
